notes: One typescript sheet, headed Commentaires Appendice, with a handwritten own-page number - 4 - and archive number 68. No date, letterhead, signature, actual mathematical diagram or display occurs. There are fourteen page-referenced comments (including the opening p.37 comment) plus the separate Donner aussi paragraph. All are transcribed. Handwriting is confined to the page number and four groups of added quotation/arrow marks in the p.5 line; its author is not established here. Two single letters have been corrected by overtyping: a by e in the p.9 nommer line, and d by e in the final paragraph. Two small detached mark groups are preserved as uncertain neutral shapes; their authored status is not asserted. The author's express questions concern detailing proof 7.4, the identity of K with raised point in 7.1, a reference for the regularity implication, seeing the argument on p.6, references for Gr with top and filtration compatibility, adding connexe in two expressions, and a source for a demonstration. The request for a diagram is a textual request, not a diagram already on this page. H is a description only, unavailable as a transcription, so every h_reading is null and every diff_h is false. The repeated cotefile wrapper in C is omitted under the current convention; that is a wrapper change, not a manuscript difference. The detached shapes use inline TikZ so their placement relative to the text and formula is retained. No theorem in the page has been proved or disproved during this reading.

The identity-arrow sentence ends with an ordinary Z and a separate underline, preserved as \underline{Z}; a blackboard alphabet is not substituted from the likely mathematical meaning.

The first Gr expression has a filled raised point and the lower roman letters top. The second has a filled raised point, empty parentheses, and a lowered underlined Q. The single Q oval and separate underline decide the alphabet against the double-struck alternative.
The references 7.3, 7.5, (7.10.2 bis), (cf. 3.3), and (7.10.1 bis) were read as printed. No arrows or diagram objects were invented from those references.
